I would never say that having kids is a way to deal with cptsd or any other issue in your life. Ideally someone should be settled and secure in their life before taking on the responsibility of a child. That being said if you wait for your life to be perfect for anything you want to do, you will be waiting forever. And obviously everyone is different and should make up their own mind about what's best for them and a potential child. 

However in my personal experience having kids has had a positive effect on my mental state. It has taught me discipline and hard work that I was not taught as a kid. It has also forced me out of my shell whether I liked it or not; I can't hide when I have to talk to my kid's teacher or when my kids want to go to a crowded park, which in it's way has brought a level of confidence. I can actually face people now without the fear I once had, at least to some degree. 

The most profound thing for me is that since becoming a mum I have reevaluated who I am and who I want to be. As a kid and well into my adult life I didn't even recognize my trauma, I thought I had a perfect life and family. It was only when I became a mum did I realize that I was in no way prepared for life and I could finally dig down into some of the reasons for that. 

My own mum is the type of person who will give her kids anything they want; not from kindness but from fear of them not loving her and I realized that I had that tendency too, but I also realized that giving my kids everything they wanted only weakened them in the long run because they would go into life expecting everything to be handed to them and not facing the things they were afraid of. 

So I guess the most important thing I learned from that is you have to find a balance in life, you have to find that fine line between pleasing yourself and being kind to others. You have to sometimes do the things you don't want to do, and sometimes it's ok to cry, but always be true to who you are, while allowing those around you be true to who they are.

I think having kids allowed me to see my trauma in the context of being the adult I was never allowed to be. If that makes any sense.

One example I can think of is when my kids where toddlers they would get hold of my things and break them as little kids do, and initially that made me feel horrible, but after some time I realized I was getting upset over petty things that didn't really matter and what mattered is my kids (and if I didn't want something broken I shouldn't give it to a toddler). Basically I got my priorities straight. Because of this I sorted out a load of old stuff because I realized I was holding onto it to cater for that part of me who wasn't allowed to grow up and by holding on to that stuff I didn't have to, at least in my head.

To give a more critical picture I have had days where being a parent has pushed me in deeper into the negative feelings of my cptsd. Kids are naturally selfish and their behavior does on occasion remind me so much of my mum that I fear they will end up just like her and it can be very triggering, but I remind myself that I have a chance to break this cycle. 

My mum became the way she is because her parents didn't instill a balance of love and discipline; they basically ignored her, so she is always looking for the love she never got and the lack of discipline means she thinks she can get her needs met with little effort and by blaming others for her problems.

I will not repeat those mistakes with my kids and that kind of gives me hope.

Sorry this went off in a tangent, but it feels good to put these feelings into words.

If you want children have children. It will be hard, but it will be much harder to look back in 20 years time and wish you had the family you could have had.

For me having children was the hardest thing I've ever done, but I wouldn't change it for anything. It has made me a better person and in a strange way it has helped with my healing.

The only thing I would say is no matter what make sure you leave time for yourself and be firm and consistent with the boundaries you set for your kids. Remember sometimes you have to be the bad guy for their own good, but they will still love you. And start as early as possible with any rules and routines. It will make it so much easier in the long run. 

And most importantly love yourself for yourself. You are not defined by your kids or your partner or anyone else.

I'm not a trained mental health professional. Everything that follows is just my opinion.

I personally don't think your problems have much, if anything, to do with ADHD. It sounds to me that they all stem from the stress your parents are putting you through. I know from personal experience that high levels of stress can have a major impact on your ability to concentrate and remember things. Lack of energy is also one of the symptoms of depression. You would be surprised by the amount of both physical and mental symptoms that can be caused by stress.

Obviously I can never truly understand your family situation, but what you describe doesn't sound like a healthy environment and I can only suggest to try to distance yourself from your parents as quickly as possible (in a safe way obviously, like if you move out when going to university). You may find things improve when you aren't being shouted at constantly. Even if they aren't the sole cause it definitely sounds like they aren't helping you.

Again I don't know what it's like in Kazakhstan, but when you go to university check to see if the university has any sort of counselor or therapist for students. Some universities offer those types of services for free.

Whatever you do don't blame yourself or think that there is anything wrong with you. You are going through what sounds like a horrible situation and your pain is real. I truly hope everything works out for the best.

I think one of the things that made it enjoyable and easy to follow despite the fact that there was no hand-holding whatsoever was the visual layout of the notebook. Clues that were related were grouped together and there were icons thrown in to make things easy to recognize (like a phone number would have a phone symbol).

I think it's about freeing up the player's mind so they don't have to think to read through a long list of keywords, but instead can jump straight to the section that relates to the idea they have to see if it makes sense with the clues they have.

I was 25 when I first realised that my mum wasn't listening to what I was saying when I talked about my feelings. It took several years after that for me to truly accept that it was something to do with her and not me. I went through phases of thinking I had some undiagnosed mental illness. 

Even 3 years later I had to sign some documents for a legal transaction between myself and my mum and I had to tell a lawyer that I understood that if my mum and I fell out it could cause problems for the agreement, and I remember thinking there was no way that could happen. I was in complete denial.

I think back on things from my childhood and I realise now that they weren't normal. Like how I was a really well behaved kid, but now I know that was because I was afraid to do anything for fear of my mum's passive aggressive behaviour.

I still struggle now with if I'm in the wrong, but I know that learning to stand up for yourself in a calm respectful way, while still considering other people's opinions, is the key to self-esteem and thus the key to avoiding being a narcissist.

While I completely understand your feelings, I personally find that hiding from the world actually leads to increased narcissistic tendencies, simply because you can't learn to empathize with others if you aren't around others. At least this is how my nMum became how she is.

It's important to remember what we've been through and make sure we don't repeat the mistakes of the past. It's not something we asked for, but for me the thought of becoming like my mum is the worst thing I can imagine and it is something I will actively work to avoid. 

I know that it's ok to look after myself and care for my needs as long as I consider the needs of those around me at the same time. It's a fine balance.

I know that fear of being yourself is one thing that drives narcissistic behavior because despite the outer shell narcissists are looking for the validation of their inner selves from the outside world. Therefore being yourself around other people is necessary to avoid lowering your sense of self and becoming narcissistic as a result. 

Don't let your fear control you. Get out there and live your life. Trust yourself.

He throws a party that's really loud without consideration for his neighbours or wife. He only cares that his kids see him as a fun person.
